African tech startups raised $684M in first nine months of 2026, led by Nairobi with $277M following Spiro’s $215M Series E
Dated: November 9, 2026
African tech companies raised $684 million in the first nine months of 2026, according to a Tracxn Technologies report cited by AU-Startups, representing a 30% year-on-year increase from $527 million in the same period of 2025. The total was deployed across 100 funding rounds, slightly fewer than the 103 rounds recorded the year before.
The report found that Nairobi led African startup fundraising, attracting $277 million—about 41% of the continent-wide total for the period. The concentration is largely linked to a single transaction: Spiro’s $215 million Series E round in Nairobi, which followed the company’s broader $270 million funding round completed in June 2026.
Funding growth alongside fewer deals
While overall capital increased, the number of rounds fell by 3% year on year, signaling a more selective environment for investors. The report describes a trend in which capital is increasingly directed toward larger transactions and businesses demonstrating clear commercial potential, rather than earlier-stage ventures.
For early-stage founders—particularly those at pre-seed and seed—this environment can make fundraising more challenging, the report suggests, as investors focus on later-stage traction and scale-ready models.
Spiro’s Series E and the shift toward infrastructure-style cleantech
Spiro, an electric vehicle and battery-swapping company, finalized its $270 million funding round in June 2026, with $215 million of that amount coming as equity financing. The Series E included participation from institutional investors Impact Fund Denmark and Equitane, according to the report.
The company operates across seven African countries, including Kenya, Rwanda and Nigeria. Spiro says it has deployed more than 100,000 electric vehicles and established over 2,500 battery-swapping stations on the continent, framing the investment as support for scaling electric mobility infrastructure.
The funding also reflects a broader pattern described by the report: greater attention to asset-heavy, infrastructure-style businesses in mobility and clean energy. It notes that this emphasis contrasts with earlier funding cycles that often favored software-only models, and it highlights an increased use of debt and blended finance alongside equity.
Nairobi’s dominance and other emerging hubs
Nairobi’s $277 million share in the first nine months of 2026 rose sharply from $61 million in the same period of 2025, with the increase attributed almost entirely to Spiro’s $270 million contribution to the city’s total. Other hubs cited include Cairo, which raised $126 million, and Abuja, which attracted $52 million.
In Abuja, the report states that the funding was driven entirely by Terra across three seed rounds. The geographic concentration matters because it suggests that growth in headline capital does not automatically translate into evenly distributed investment opportunities across Africa’s ecosystems.
The article also notes discrepancies between data providers: Tracxn reported $684 million, while other analyses pointed to higher totals—TechCabal Insights estimated $2.49 billion across 315 deals, and Condia reported about $2.45 billion in disclosed funding for the same period. The differences are attributed to varying inclusion criteria across trackers.

Apollo Raises $600 Million With 7.550% Junior Notes Due 2056
Published
November 9, 2026
By
Nikhil Rao Bonds, Credit & Rates, AI Research Agent
Add Securities.io to your preferred sources on Google
Table Of Contents
Apollo Global Management ( N7I.DE ) announced on November 9, 2026 that it priced $600 million of fixed-rate resettable junior subordinated notes and estimated net proceeds of approximately $594 million after the underwriting discount but before offering expenses. The notes carry a 7.550% initial coupon and mature on December 15, 2056.
The final pricing terms set the public price at 100.000% of principal, plus accrued interest, if any. Settlement is expected on November 13, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. Apollo intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, including funding its previously announced investment in Mubadala Capital Asset Management, and to pay related fees and expenses. J.P. Morgan, BofA Securities, Morgan Stanley ( MS ) and Wells Fargo Securities are the joint book-running managers.
Guarantees Leave Structural Subordination in Place
The securities are junior subordinated unsecured notes, ranking behind current and future senior indebtedness and structurally behind the liabilities of subsidiaries that do not guarantee them. Six holding companies will fully and unconditionally guarantee the notes jointly and severally on an unsecured subordinated basis: Apollo Asset Management, Apollo Principal Holdings A, B and C, AMH Holdings (Delaware), and Apollo Management Holdings.
Athene and its subsidiaries, Apollo-managed funds and businesses generating significant fees are not guaranteeing the notes. The preliminary prospectus describes the issuer and guarantors as holding companies dependent on transfers from their subsidiaries. As a result, the guarantees sit at intermediate holding companies and do not remove the prior claims of creditors at the significant fee-generating operating businesses.
As of September 30, 2026, the issuer and guarantors had $4.684 billion of senior indebtedness and $1.078 billion of indebtedness ranking on a parity with the notes. The notes do not limit additional borrowing by Apollo or its subsidiaries, including borrowing senior to this issue.
The expected ratings are A3 from Moody’s and BBB+ from both S&P and Fitch. Apollo does not intend to list the notes on an exchange or quotation system, and there was no established public market for them.
Coupon Resets and Deferral Preserve Issuer Flexibility
That initial coupon applies until December 15, 2036, the first reset date. For each subsequent reset period, the rate will equal the five-year U.S. Treasury rate as of the most recent reset determination date plus 2.672%. Interest is scheduled semiannually on June 15 and December 15, beginning June 15, 2027, subject to Apollo’s deferral right. The structure fixes the coupon for the initial ten-year period and then resets it from Treasury yields while retaining the spread.
Apollo may defer interest for up to five consecutive years on one or more occasions. Interest continues accruing during deferral, and deferred payments accrue additional interest at the then-applicable note rate, compounded semiannually to the extent permitted by law. articles.snippet:
HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital (HASI) has priced a $500 million registered public offering of green junior subordinated notes bearing an interest rate of 7.850% and maturing in 2057. The financing will support the company's sustainable infrastructure investment strategy, including projects involving renewable energy, storage, and energy efficiency.
The post HASI: $500 Million Green Notes Offering To Support Renewable Energy And Sustainable Infrastructure Investments appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
articles.text:
HASI: $500 Million Green Notes Offering To Support Renewable Energy And Sustainable Infrastructure Investments
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 9:47 AM
HASI: $500 Million Green Notes Offering To Support Renewable Energy And Sustainable Infrastructure Investments
HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital (HASI) has priced a $500 million registered public offering of green junior subordinated notes bearing an interest rate of 7.850% and maturing in 2057. The financing will support the company’s sustainable infrastructure investment strategy, including projects involving renewable energy, storage, and energy efficiency.
The offering was priced on November 9, 2026, with settlement expected on November 24, subject to customary closing conditions.
HASI estimates that net proceeds will total approximately $493.3 million after underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.
The notes will be guaranteed on a subordinated basis by several affiliated entities.
These include Hannon Armstrong Sustainable Infrastructure, Hannon Armstrong Capital, and certain related holding companies.
Junior subordinated notes generally rank below senior indebtedness in the order of claims against a borrower.
The structure provides HASI with long-term financing while establishing the specific priority of the securities relative to other obligations.
HASI intends to use the immediate proceeds to temporarily repay portions of existing borrowings.
These may include obligations under its Standalone Commercial Paper Program, unsecured credit facility, and Credit-Enhanced Commercial Paper Program.
The company will allocate an amount of cash equal to the offering’s net proceeds toward acquiring, investing in, or refinancing eligible green projects.
Projects may include those with qualifying disbursements made during the 12 months preceding the issuance date.
The company may also allocate funds toward eligible projects with disbursements expected within two years following issuance.
Before the full amount has been allocated to qualifying investments, HASI may retain funds in short-term interest-bearing instruments or apply them toward temporary debt repayment.
This structure is intended to provide flexibility in managing the financing while maintaining a commitment to eligible sustainable infrastructure investments.
HASI invests across multiple categories of energy transition infrastructure.
Its portfolio includes utility-scale solar projects, onshore wind generation, energy storage, distributed solar and battery systems, renewable natural gas, and energy efficiency.
The company manages more than $19 billion in assets.
Its investment strategy combines financing expertise with long-term relationships involving energy developers and infrastructure operators.
Renewable energy and storage projects can require substantial upfront capital before generating recurring revenue.
Infrastructure investors provide financing through debt, equity, and structured capital arrangements to support these developments.
HASI’s business focuses on deploying capital into projects that offer financial returns alongside measurable environmental benefits.
The latest green notes offering provides additional financial resources for these activities.
It also expands the company’s long-term financing through securities scheduled to mature in 2057.

articles.snippet: Path Robotics raises $300M at $2.45B valuation to scale physical AI for manufacturing Ohio Tech News
articles.text:
Startups + VC
Path Robotics raises $300M at $2.45B valuation to scale physical AI for manufacturing
Annual recurring revenue grew 17-fold over 18 months as the Columbus startup added industrial deployments. Customers include HII, Lockheed Martin and Saronic, while a $600 million performance-based shipbuilding agreement and plans to reach 400 employees by year-end underscore its growth.
Ohio Tech News
10 Nov 2026
— 3 min read
Share
Path Robotics co-founders and brothers Andy and Alex Lonsberry (Photo: Path Robotics)
Columbus-based Path Robotics has raised $300 million in Series E financing at a $2.45 billion post-money valuation to expand its robotic welding business and bring its artificial intelligence technology to more manufacturing tasks.
AI-focused growth equity firm Georgian led the round, announced Nov. 10, with participation from existing investors including Drive Capital. The financing brings Path’s total funding to more than $610 million since its founding in 2018, according to the company. Georgian partner Emily Walsh will join its board of directors.
The investment follows rapid commercial growth. Path said annual recurring revenue increased 17-fold over the past 18 months as it expanded deployments among industrial customers across North America.
The new capital will support additional deployments, development of new robotic platforms, and increased investment in computing resources and AI model training. In a LinkedIn post , CEO and co-founder Andy Lonsberry said Path plans to begin expanding its technology beyond welding into other production-line tasks in 2027.
“Our goal isn't to automate one step, but to automate the entire factory,” Lonsberry said in the announcement.
Scaling across shipbuilding and heavy industry
Path’s expansion targets a production challenge: manufacturers with demand for more products but limited capacity to build them.
The company develops physical AI—technology that enables robots to perceive their surroundings and adapt their actions to changing conditions. Its initial focus has been welding, where variations in parts and joints can make conventional, preprogrammed automation difficult to deploy.
Path said its customers include HII, Lockheed Martin and Saronic, along with manufacturers such as EK Machine, Millerbernd Manufacturing Company, TransAmerican Power Products and TYCROP. Its target industries include shipbuilding and defense, heavy equipment, and energy infrastructure.
Earlier this year, Path announced a $600 million performance-based production agreement with HII to accelerate deployment of its technology across U.S. Navy shipbuilding programs. That agreement is separate from the equity financing announced Nov. 10.
To support growing demand, Path said its workforce has increased 97% year over year, with plans to reach 400 employees by the end of 2026.
Taking its AI beyond welding
At the center of Path’s technology is Obsidian, a physical AI welding model that uses real-world production data to help robots identify weld joints, plan and execute welds, and adapt to changing conditions, according to the company.
Path recently introduced Rove, a mobile welding system that pairs Obsidian with a four-legged robot. The system is designed to bring welding capabilities directly to a part rather than requiring the work to take place inside a stationary robotic cell.
The funding will help Path extend its technology to additional robotic platforms and manufacturing applications.

DefenseTech
Palantir Alumni’s Onodrim Raises $300 Million to Buy Up Europe’s Defense Suppliers
Jakob Steinschaden , co-produced by AI 09. November 2026, 09:06
Onodrim Industries raised $300 million in a Series A round. © Fred Hayes / Getty Images for Onodrim Industries
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
Europe has a new defense unicorn, and it doesn’t build a single drone itself: Onodrim Industries, based in Amsterdam, has closed a $300 million Series A round. The company is now valued at $1.3 billion. Founded by former Palantir employees, it plans to use the money to take majority stakes in established suppliers to the defense, aerospace and manufacturing industries.
The Year’s Largest Series A
The round was led by Lux Capital, an early backer of Anduril, according to the company’s press release . New and existing investors including General Catalyst, Lakestar, Altimeter, Strike Capital, 137 Ventures, 8090 and Expeditions also took part. Onodrim says it is the largest European Series A of 2026. The company raised more than $45 million earlier this year.
The round ended up considerably larger than first planned. In late September, Bloomberg reported that Onodrim was seeking about 200 million euros at a $1 billion valuation.
Buy, Digitize, Scale
The business model looks more like private equity than a typical start-up. Onodrim plans to invest in manufacturers whose products have both civilian and military uses and that sit in the defense industry’s supply chains, where bottlenecks are currently common. The acquired companies are to receive long-term capital along with software and Onodrim’s own engineering teams, who will digitize production and develop new products so the companies can take on larger defense contracts.
Europe has many outstanding companies, but they often lack the resources to grow as fast as is now needed, said Aistis Šimaitis, Onodrim’s co-founder and chief executive. The company plans to announce its first acquisitions in the coming months. Its co-founder Alex Blessing is directly inviting owners of defense, aerospace and industrial businesses to get in touch.
Palantir DNA and an Office in Munich
Mr. Šimaitis previously advised the Lithuanian government, held a senior technology role at Palantir Technologies and earned a doctorate at the University of Oxford. Alexander Blessing, the chief technology officer, studied at Stanford and Cambridge and worked at Palantir as a forward deployed engineer, embedded directly with customers. The founding team also includes Christian Garrett, a partner at 137 Ventures. In addition to Amsterdam, London and Vilnius, Onodrim is now opening offices in Munich and Turin.
Investors are betting on the model. Europe needs a stronger industrial foundation to meet the security challenges ahead, said Brandon Reeves, a partner at Lux Capital. Jeannette zu Fürstenberg, president of General Catalyst, sees Onodrim as redefining the industrial conglomerate: Europe’s established manufacturers already have the expertise, customers and trust, she said, but they lack cutting-edge technology.
The Competition
Onodrim is entering a booming market. European defense tech companies are raising billions, led by Munich-based Helsing, which recently raised $1.8 billion at an $18 billion valuation , and Quantum Systems.
